source.dataset: Comte, L., Grenouillet, G., Bertrand, R., Murienne, J., Bourgeaud, L., Hattab, T. & Lenoir, J. (2020) BioShifts: a global geodatabase of climate-induced species redistribution over land and sea. Figshare.
source.paper: Lenoir, J., Bertrand, R., Comte, L., Bourgeaud, L., Hattab, T., Murienne, J. & Grenouillet, G. (2020) Species better track climate warming in the oceans than on land. Nature Ecology & Evolution 4, 1044-1059.
source.signConvention: kmYr > 0 means the range moved poleward (north in the Northern Hemisphere, south in the Southern); < 0 means equatorward. Coded this way by the BioShifts compilers (Lenoir et al. 2020, Methods); rates are the published shift divided by the study duration.
source.scope: Marine records only; all are latitudinal (studies of depth-only or longitude-only shifts were excluded by the compilers). Each record is one species x range position (C centroid, L leading/poleward edge, T trailing/equatorward edge) x study area x period, taken from a published study.
source.points: Planar centroid of the study-area polygon, rounded to 0.1 deg; it can fall on land for coastal studies. bbox is [west, south, east, north]; west > east means it crosses the antimeridian.
source.paperHeadline: Lenoir et al. 2020 report marine species moving poleward at 5.92 +/- 0.94 km/yr (mean +/- s.e.m. of class-level estimates from mixed models that correct for methodological differences), about six times faster than terrestrial species. The raw-record medians and means here are simpler and lower.
source.caveat: Study areas are heavily concentrated in the North Atlantic (North Sea, NE US shelf, Iberia) and North Pacific (Bering Sea, California Current, Japan). The tropics, the Indian Ocean, Africa, South America and the Southern Ocean are barely sampled, so the map shows where scientists have looked, not where species are moving.

classLabels.Liliopsida: monocot plants (as classified; Acmira catherinae here is almost certainly the polychaete homonym)

source.arrows: Arrows point towards the pole or the equator, with length scaled to the area's median shift. They are shortened where they would cross land; areas whose centroid falls on land are drawn from the nearest sea point.
